sourceNote: Case constructed from public SEC filings (10-K and 10-Q) and investor materials for a mid-tier department store chain, financial data covering FY2022-FY2025. All figures from publicly available disclosures; no proprietary internal data and no answer-key content embedded in this input.

ownerIntake.businessType: Mid-tier department store chain operating 45 full-line stores across suburban and secondary markets. ~$800M annual revenue, ~6,500 employees. Apparel, home goods, beauty, and accessories under a single banner. Public company.
ownerIntake.stage: Revenue declined from $850M (FY2023) to $800M (FY2025), a 5.9% drop. EBITDA margin fell from 6% to 4% (-200 bps). Same-store sales down ~4% per year. Inventory growing faster than sales (inventory up ~12% over two years on declining revenue). E-commerce only ~14% of sales versus ~30%+ for stronger peers.
ownerIntake.ownerGoal: Stabilize profitability and avoid a wave of store closures or a distressed sale. Restore EBITDA margin toward 6% and right-size the store base and inventory to actual demand within 24 months.
ownerConstraints: Secular constraint: Brick-and-mortar department-store foot traffic is in structural decline; the company built and staffed a 45-store footprint sized for demand that no longer materializes at the planned level.
Competitive constraint: E-commerce and off-price competitors (Amazon, Target, TJX) are capturing the chain's traditional mid-tier shopper; the company cannot match their assortment breadth or price.
Cost constraint: High fixed real-estate (long-term leases) and store-labor costs do not flex down as revenue and traffic fall, de-leveraging margin.
Inventory constraint: Buying and allocation are still planned to a higher demand forecast, leaving excess seasonal inventory that must be cleared at markdown, compressing gross margin.
Capital constraint: Limited balance-sheet flexibility; major store closures carry lease-termination costs and require careful investor communication to avoid signaling distress.
ownerIntake.immediateConcern: Same-store sales keep declining while inventory accumulates and markdowns deepen, indicating the company is buying and operating to a demand level that the market is no longer delivering. Margin is compressing because fixed store and lease costs are spread over a shrinking, over-forecasted revenue base. The core question is whether the store footprint and inventory plan are sized to real, sustainable demand or to an outdated forecast.

Gross margin and markdown rate by category (investor presentations)
Store-level metrics: sales per store, sales per square foot, traffic trends
Inventory levels and inventory turnover (balance sheet, MD&A)
Channel mix: in-store vs e-commerce revenue split

clientContext.revenueImpactUrgency: CRITICAL (declining sales, accumulating inventory, and margin compression threaten viability and risk a distressed outcome)

businessProblem: A mid-tier department store chain is declining: revenue fell from $850M (FY2023) to $800M (FY2025) and EBITDA margin compressed from 6% to 4%. Same-store sales decline ~4% per year while inventory accumulates (+~12%) and markdowns deepen, indicating the company is buying and operating its 45-store footprint to a demand forecast that the market no longer delivers. Fixed real-estate and store-labor costs do not flex down, so margin de-leverages as revenue shrinks. The central question: is the deterioration a structural mismatch between the company's demand/footprint plan and actual sustainable demand (over-forecasted store base and inventory), a competitive displacement problem, or a pure cost-structure problem? Without store-level demand and contribution analysis, the chain risks either closing the wrong stores or continuing to overbuy inventory against an outdated forecast.

evidence.finding: Revenue declined from $850M (FY2023) to $800M (FY2025), a 5.9% decrease, while EBITDA margin fell from 6% to 4% (-200 bps). EBITDA fell from ~$51M to ~$32M (-37%). The margin decline outpaces the revenue decline, indicating fixed costs are not flexing down as the demand base shrinks.

Same-store sales declined approximately 4% per year over the period, indicating demand contraction at the existing footprint rather than a one-time shock. The 45-store base was sized and staffed for a higher demand level that is no longer materializing, leaving stores under-trafficked.
evidence.source: Investor presentations and 10-K MD&A (same-store sales disclosure)

evidence.finding: Inventory grew approximately 12% over two years while revenue fell 5.9%, so inventory turnover deteriorated and markdown rates rose. Buying and allocation remained planned to a higher demand forecast than the market delivered, leaving excess seasonal inventory cleared at markdown and compressing gross margin.
evidence.source: Balance sheet (inventory), MD&A (markdown commentary), category margin disclosure

evidence.finding: E-commerce is only ~14% of the chain's sales versus ~30%+ for stronger department-store peers, while off-price and online competitors (Amazon, Target, TJX) capture the mid-tier shopper. The traditional in-store demand the footprint was forecast against is migrating to channels and competitors the company under-serves.
evidence.source: Investor presentations (channel mix), public peer benchmarking
